title: Bargain Hard
coreMove: Hold the price conversation firmly without collapsing into a split-the-difference compromise.
sourcePressure: The source ties this chapter to price negotiation, haggling, non-round numbers, strategic umbrage, and resisting simple compromise after agreement has survived execution pressure.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer must not turn bargaining hard into aggression, bravado, or a guaranteed formula based on precise numbers.

exampleSpecs.domain: marine salvage contract after a disabled research vessel
exampleSpecs.audience: a university procurement officer bargaining with a salvage firm under time pressure
exampleSpecs.stakes: equipment losses grow each tide, but accepting the first midpoint would erase the lab's repair budget
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the officer anchors with a specific mobilization number tied to tug hours and refuses the simple midpoint until the firm separates standby fees from lift fees
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a wet salvage estimate clipped to a chart table beside tide notes

exampleSpecs.domain: boutique textile mill negotiating a loom repair invoice
exampleSpecs.audience: a mill owner challenging a repair vendor's bundled charge
exampleSpecs.stakes: paying the full invoice may consume cash needed for next month's wool purchase
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner shows calibrated umbrage at the bundled total, then offers a non-round number based on parts actually logged
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a broken heddle frame resting on a canvas drop cloth near a silent loom

exampleSpecs.domain: regional ambulance service fuel surcharge negotiation
exampleSpecs.audience: a county contract officer bargaining with a private ambulance provider
exampleSpecs.stakes: a vague surcharge could drain funds from rural coverage hours
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the officer reviews how refusing the rounded surcharge and presenting a cents-per-mile counter forced the provider to reveal idle-time assumptions
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a fuel receipt taped to a route-mileage sheet beside a dispatch radio

exampleSpecs.domain: translation-rights auction for a niche technical manual
exampleSpecs.audience: a small publisher bargaining with an overseas rights agent
exampleSpecs.stakes: a careless split could give away rights that matter more than the advance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the publisher reacts to the agent's bundle as unacceptable, then separates territory, term length, and glossary ownership instead of meeting at the middle advance
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a rights grid printed beside a marked-up glossary page

exampleSpecs.domain: catering equipment lease after a venue policy change
exampleSpecs.audience: a caterer renegotiating refrigeration fees with an event venue
exampleSpecs.stakes: absorbing the new fee would wipe out profit on three booked weddings
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the caterer moves from arguing fairness to a precise counter tied to actual compressor hours and refuses a round halfway concession
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a compressor-hour meter glowing inside a walk-in trailer

exampleSpecs.audience: an artistic director bargaining with a musicians' representative over rehearsal pay
exampleSpecs.stakes: splitting the difference may still leave the orchestra unwilling to cover added tech rehearsals
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director refuses the midpoint frame and counters with a non-round package that trades rehearsal blocks, meal penalties, and matinee call times
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a marked rehearsal schedule tucked under a bass bow on the pit rail

skillTargets: apply non-round numbers as evidence of calculation rather than magic
analyze why midpoint compromise can destroy key terms
evaluate when strategic umbrage is warranted or performative

tryThisNowSpec: Before accepting any midpoint, list the separate terms hidden inside the price, calculate one non-round counter from a real cost, and decide which term you will not average away.
sourceAnchorsNote: source contains no named anecdote for this chapter
